sec.t:
Ctesias said the horn of the Indian beast could cure poisoning. Later, the Roman writer Pliny the Elder described a "monoceros", meaning one-horn, with a horse's body, an elephant's feet and a deep bellow. That sounds less like a fairy-tale pony and more like a rhino.

The Indian rhino really does have one horn. It lives in grasslands in Assam and Nepal today. Its horn is made of [[keratin|keratin]], the same [[protein|protein]] as your fingernails, not bone. A garbled description passed from trader to trader across Persia and Greece could easily turn a heavy grey animal into something more magical.

sec.h: The one-horned animal on Indus seals

sec.t:
In [[medieval|medieval]] Europe, "unicorn horns" were among the most precious things a king could own. They were long, white and spiralled. They were believed to detect poison, and some were worth more than their weight in gold.

They were really tusks of the narwhal, a whale from the Arctic. A male narwhal's tusk is an overgrown tooth that can grow longer than a tall man is tall. Viking and later traders sold them without explaining their source. Denmark's royal throne, made in the 1600s, is built largely from narwhal tusks. By the 1600s, as more people saw narwhals, scientists began to see through the trick.

sec.h: A unicorn on the royal arms
sec.t:
Scotland adopted the unicorn as a royal symbol in the 1400s, and it is still the country's national animal. In stories, the unicorn was proud and could not be tamed, which suited a kingdom that valued its freedom. When Scotland and England shared a king from 1603, the royal coat of arms showed a lion and a unicorn side by side.

Asia has its own one-horned creatures too. The Chinese qilin, sometimes called a unicorn in English, is a gentle beast whose arrival was said to signal a wise ruler.

Today, unicorns are everywhere: on lunchboxes, cakes and cartoons. In business, a "unicorn" is a young company worth a billion US dollars, a name chosen because such companies were once very rare. India and the USA now have many of them. A unicorn face was added to the official emoji set in 2015, and it quickly became a favourite for birthday messages.

And the strangest part? A giant hairy rhino with a huge single horn, nicknamed the "Siberian unicorn", really did roam Asia until tens of thousands of years ago, at the same time as early humans. Stories of [[@myths-dragons|dragons]] may also have begun with real bones.

text: A poem is writing that pays special attention to sound, [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]] and shape, as well as meaning. Prose, like this paragraph, runs on until the edge of the page. A poem is usually broken into lines, and the poet decides exactly where each one ends.

Most poems use some of these tools: a beat, rhyme, repeated sounds, vivid pictures in words, and a lot of meaning packed into few words. No one tool is required. Experts have argued for centuries about where poetry stops and prose begins. In the end, a poem is writing that asks you to read slowly and listen.

st.prompt: Who is the earliest author in history whose name we know?

options.t: Enheduanna, a priestess and poet in Mesopotamia
Homer, the Greek poet
Valmiki, poet of the Ramayana

st.reveal: Enheduanna lived in the city of Ur around 2300 BCE. Hymns to the moon god and the goddess Inanna carry her name. Some scholars wonder whether all of them are really hers, but she is still the earliest named author on record.

src: Poetry Foundation, glossary of poetic terms.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, poetry.
n.certNote: There is no single definition of poetry that every expert accepts. Rhythm, line breaks and rich language are common features, but poets keep breaking each rule.

d.try: Take a sentence from your science or history book and rewrite it as a poem. Break it into short lines wherever you would pause, swap one dull word for a vivid one and read it aloud. You may find a poem was hiding in it all along.
myth: A poem has to rhyme.
Many poems don't rhyme at all. Most old Sanskrit, Greek and Latin poetry doesn't, and neither do haiku or modern free verse. Rhythm and careful word choice matter more than rhyme.

poetry without a fixed beat or rhyme

sec.t:
Poetry is older than writing. Before people could write things down, they needed a way to remember laws, prayers, family histories and stories. [[rhythm|Rhythm]] and repetition make words stick in the [[@memory|memory]]. That is why you can recall song lyrics far more easily than a shopping list.

The oldest named author we know of, Enheduanna, was a poet. She was a priestess in the city of Ur in [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] around 2300 BCE, and hymns carrying her name were copied by scribes for centuries. In India, the hymns of the Rigveda were composed in the [[@vedic-age|Vedic age]] and passed on by heart, in exact rhythms, long before they were written down.

In the south, the Tamil poems of the Sangam period, roughly 2,000 years old, sorted the land into five types: hills, forest, farmland, seashore and dry wasteland. Each landscape went with a mood, such as lovers meeting in the hills or waiting by the sea. A single flower named in a poem could tell readers where they were and how to feel.

**Rhythm** is the pattern of strong and weak beats. [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] poets built strict metres, like the shloka, which has four quarters of eight [[syllable|syllables]] each. Tradition says the sage Valmiki spoke the first shloka in grief after seeing a hunter kill a bird, and went on to compose the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] in that metre.

**Rhyme** is the matching of end sounds, like "moon" and "June". It is common in English, Hindi and Urdu poems and songs.

**Imagery** means pictures made of words. "The fog comes on little cat feet" is the American poet Carl Sandburg's way of showing fog creeping silently in.

**Compression** means saying a lot in a little. A two-line doha by Kabir or a three-line [[@haiku|haiku]] can hold a whole idea.

{{story:hip-hop}}

For most of history, poems were performed aloud, often with music. The [[bhakti|bhakti]] poets [[@mirabai-kabir|Mirabai and Kabir]] composed verses that are still sung in homes and temples across India. [[@ghazals|Ghazals]] in Urdu and Persian are sung at concerts. Many [[@film-songs|film songs]] are poems set to tunes.

Rap is a modern example. [[@hip-hop|Hip-hop]] artists use rhythm, rhyme and wordplay as carefully as any poet, often with rhymes inside lines as well as at the end. Some universities now study rap lyrics alongside older poetry.

In 1855, the American poet Walt Whitman published Leaves of Grass. It used long, loose lines without regular rhyme or metre, a style now called free verse. Many readers were shocked. Today, free verse is probably the most common kind of poem written in English.

Poets keep finding new shapes. Some make "concrete poems", where the words are arranged into a picture. Some write prose poems that look like ordinary paragraphs. Whether something counts as a poem is often settled by how it makes readers listen.

text: Biryani is a dish of fragrant rice layered with spiced meat, fish, eggs or vegetables, then cooked slowly in a sealed pot. Most historians think it grew out of [[@ancient-persia|Persian]] rice dishes like pilaf. Cooks at the courts of the [[@mughals|Mughals]] and the sultans of the Deccan brought them to India from the 1500s onwards.

In India, those dishes met local spices, local rice and local cooks. Over time, every region that took up biryani changed it. That is why there isn't one biryani but dozens. Each tastes of the place where it grew up.

st.prompt: In dum cooking, what do cooks traditionally use to seal the lid of the biryani pot?

options.t: A rope of wheat dough pressed around the rim
Melted wax
Wet clay from a riverbank

st.reveal: A strip of dough is pressed between lid and pot to make an airtight seal. Steam can't escape, so the rice and meat cook slowly in their own juices and smells. When the dough is broken, a cloud of fragrant steam bursts out.

src: Achaya K.T. A Historical Dictionary of Indian Food. Oxford University Press, 1998.

src.Collingham L. Curry: A Tale of Cooks and Conquerors. Oxford University Press, 2006.

n.certNote: Most food historians link biryani to Persian cooking brought to India by Mughal and Deccan courts. Others point to older Indian rice-and-meat dishes, such as the Tamil oon soru, and to Arab traders on the Kerala coast. No one recipe can be called the first.

myth: Biryani and pulao are the same dish with different names.

They are close cousins. In a pulao, rice and meat or vegetables usually cook together in one go. In a biryani, the rice is usually part-cooked separately and layered with the meat or vegetables, then finished on dum. Cooks argue happily about the exact line.

sec.t:
The word biryani is usually traced to Persian. *Birinj* means rice, and *biryan* means fried or roasted. Persian cooks made pilafs of rice and meat, and these travelled with soldiers, traders and nobles into India.

At royal courts, cooks had time and money to experiment. They added [[@saffron|saffron]], rose water, ghee and many spices. The Mughal court and the courts of the Deccan, especially Golconda near Hyderabad, developed rich, layered rice dishes that became biryani.

Not everyone agrees that biryani came only from Persia. Old Tamil poems describe *oon soru*, rice cooked with meat, ghee and spices, eaten by warriors. Arab traders sailed to the [[@kerala|Kerala]] coast for centuries and brought their own rice dishes.

Some food historians think these older traditions mixed with Persian ideas. Others say they were different dishes that later borrowed the name biryani. Both points of view have supporters, and the evidence isn't enough to settle it. Food and recipes often travel along [[@trade-routes|trade routes]] without leaving clear records.

Biryani's key cooking method is called dum, meaning breath or steam. The meat is marinated in curd and spices, and the rice is partly boiled. They are layered in a heavy pot, sprinkled with saffron milk, fried onions and ghee. The lid is sealed with a rope of dough.

The pot is cooked slowly on low heat, sometimes with hot coals on the lid. Trapped steam finishes cooking the rice and carries the smells of meat and spice through every grain. When the dough seal is broken at the table, the steam rushes out.

Biryani is now one of the most ordered dishes on food delivery apps in India, year after year. It is cooked in huge pots at weddings and at Eid. Vegetarian versions, with [[@cheese-paneer|paneer]], mushrooms or vegetables, are popular too, though some people insist that only pulao can be vegetarian.

Biryani has followed Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis around the world. You'll find it in Dubai, London, Toronto and New Jersey. There it is cooked by families from many regions, each sure that their grandmother's [[@rice|rice]] is the best.

text: Guavas and papayas first grew in the warm forests of southern Mexico, Central America and northern South America. People there were eating them long before Europeans arrived.

After [[@columbus|Columbus]] crossed the Atlantic in 1492, Spanish and [[@portuguese-india|Portuguese]] sailors carried American plants around the world. Guavas and papayas travelled across oceans along with chillies, tomatoes, potatoes and corn. They probably reached India in the 1500s and 1600s, and loved the warm [[climate|climate]] so much that they grew almost everywhere. Today India grows more guavas and more papayas than any other country.

st.prompt: Guavas and papayas came to India from the Americas. Which of these also came from there?

options.t: Chilli
Mango
Banana

st.reveal: Chillies came from Mexico and Central America, and reached India with Portuguese traders, just like guavas and papayas. Mangoes come from India itself, and bananas first grew in Southeast Asia and New Guinea.

a giant herb, not a true tree

sec.t:
Guava trees are small and tough. They grow in poor soil, survive dry spells and fruit twice a year. Their fruit can be white or pink inside, packed with small hard seeds, and smells strongly sweet when ripe.

In India, guava is called amrood or peru in many places. Street sellers slice it and sprinkle it with salt and red chilli powder, which makes the sweet fruit taste even sweeter. Prayagraj, formerly Allahabad, is famous for a variety called Allahabad Safeda.

Weight for weight, guava has about four times as much [[@vitamins|vitamin C]] as an orange. Your body needs [[vitamin|vitamin]] C to heal cuts and keep gums healthy, and it can't store much, so you need some every day.

A papaya plant looks like a palm tree, but it isn't a tree at all. It is a giant herb with a soft, hollow stem and a crown of big leaves at the top. It can grow from a seed to a fruiting plant in less than a year, which is very fast for a plant that size.

Papaya fruit hangs in clusters right under the leaves. Inside, the flesh is orange and soft, with a hollow full of shiny black seeds that taste peppery. Green papaya is cooked as a vegetable or grated into salads in many parts of India and Southeast Asia.

Unripe papaya is full of an [[enzyme|enzyme]] called papain, which breaks down [[protein|proteins]]. Cooks in India have long added raw papaya paste to meat to make it tender, and papain is used in some meat tenderiser powders.

In the 1990s, a virus called papaya ringspot spread through papaya farms in [[@hawaii-culture|Hawaii]]. It made the plants weak and the fruit spotty, and the industry was close to collapse. Scientists at the University of Hawaii and Cornell University developed a papaya that resists the virus by giving it a small piece of the virus's own [[gene|genes]], a little like a [[vaccine|vaccine]].

Farmers began planting this "Rainbow" papaya in 1998, and Hawaiian papaya farming recovered. It is one of the best-known examples of a genetically modified crop helping farmers, though people still debate whether such crops should be grown.

Both fruits now grow wild in many [[tropical|tropical]] places they weren't native to. Guava trees spread so well that they have become a weed in some islands, crowding out local plants. In India, though, they mostly stay in gardens, orchards and street carts. It's strange to think that a fruit sold from a handcart outside an Indian school first ripened in a forest on the other side of the world.
